newsitem.title: ISRAEL: No quick fix seen from Israeli economic measures.
newsitem.headline: No quick fix seen from Israeli economic measures.

text.p: The economic measures taken by Israel's government over the last 24 hours were praiseworthy but would produce no dramatic changes in the exchange rate or economic growth, economists and analysts said.

In a series of late-night meetings between top economic policy makers, the government announced it would take measures to liberalise foreign currency regulations over the next year with the aim of making the Israeli currency nearly convertible.

Early on Wednesday morning, the cabinet approved plans to widen the shekel's trading band and adjust its sloping midpoint -- a controversial decision that led to Finance Minister Dan Meridor's resignation. At noon on Wednesday, the Bank of Israel announced a sharp 1.2 percentage point cut in the base rate to 12.7 percent.
"All told, I think the moves are very positive," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets, adding however that he was concerned about the size of the rate cut.
"There was definitely room for monetary loosening, but I though he should have played slightly more cautiously."

Economists agreed that the measures would not significantly affect the exchange rate for the short term. The shekel has been trading at the bottom end of its old trading band against a basket of foreign currencies all this year, as capital flowed into the country to take advantage of Israel's high interest rates.
When the shekel is at the bottom end of its trading band this means it is strong as it takes less shekels to buy basket currencies.
Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg, an economist with Bank Hapoalim, said the interest rate cut announced on Wednesday would be insufficient to stem the capital inflows.
She added that while the upper end of the trading band had been widened to 15 percent from seven percent, the lower end remained unchanged.
She said that would force the Bank of Israel to continue intervening in the market to defend the shekel as it has all this year, although on a smaller scale.
"We expect the exchange to continue crawling along the bottom limit of the band, but now at a slower pace of four percent annually," she said in a report.
Economists were mixed about the impact of the measures on Israel's economy, which has registered sluggish growth over the last year.

"I don't think it will bring the economy out of its slowdown, but I think we are already at the nadir," said Shauli Katznelson, chief economist at Israel Discount Bank, who is holding to his forecasts of 2.7 percent growth this year and three percent next year.
Katz said he expected the shekel to gradually depreciate as the effects of the foreign currency liberalisation measures kicked in.
The reforms will give corporate and institutional investors, as well as individuals, greater freedom to invest and hold money abroad, thereby encouraging currency outflows.
Daniel Carasso, Israel analyst for UBS Securities, agreed, adding that a depreciation would be a boost for Israeli companies and the stock market.

"Whether or not the shekel stregthens or weakens in the initial days and weeks, it ultimately should weaken to the benefit of corporate Israel, particularly exporters like ECI Telecom, Israel Chemicals group and Teva TEV1001.TA," Carasso said.
But the positive impact of the economic measures could be clouded by worries about Meridor's successor as finance minister, analysts warned.
National Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon and former justice minister Yaacov Neeman are being rumoured as the two leading candidates.

Katz warned that the markets would be nervous with a Sharon appointment for fear the populist ex-general would not maintain budgetary restraint. But Carasso said Netanyahu was unlikely to pick a budget-busting finance minister.
"Any cabinet reshuffle is unlikely to have a negative impact on the positive capital market direction (privatisation, balancing the budget, reducing inflation etc.)."
